drug_class: Targeted therapy / EGFR inhibitor (a type of cancer medicine)
purpose: Erlotinib is used to treat certain types of non-small cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer. It is especially helpful for lung cancers that have a specific gene change called an EGFR mutation. Your doctor will test your tumor to see if this medicine is right for you.
how_it_works: Cancer cells sometimes have a protein on their surface called EGFR that tells them to grow out of control. Erlotinib works like a key that blocks this protein, so the cancer cells can no longer get the signal to keep growing. Think of it as putting a cap on the switch that turns cancer growth on.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include a skin rash (often on your face and chest), dry or cracked skin, diarrhea, feeling tired, loss of appetite, nausea, and mouth sores. Many people also get dry or irritated eyes. The skin rash is very common but usually manageable with creams and care.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have sudden shortness of breath, a new or worsening cough, or chest pain, as this could be a rare but serious lung problem. Erlotinib can harm an unborn baby, so do not become pregnant while taking it. It can also cause serious liver problems, so your doctor will monitor your blood tests regularly. Avoid smoking while taking this medicine, as it can make the drug less effective.
typical_dosing: For lung cancer, the usual dose is one 150 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day. For pancreatic cancer, the usual dose is one 100 mg tablet once a day. It should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, at the same time each day. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water.
